Earle, Physical Geology 2nd ed. (BCcampus), 10.4 Plates, Plate Motions, and Plate Boundary Processes
Earle, Physical Geology 2nd ed. (BCcampus), 1.5 Fundamentals of Plate Tectonics

steps.title: Two plates
steps.instruction: Trace the two plates in picture 1.

note.text: Earth's outer shell is broken into about 20 plates that move a few centimetres a year.

steps.title: Moving apart
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows showing the plates moving apart.

note.text: Here the plates spread apart. This is a divergent boundary.

steps.title: Rising magma
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of magma rising between them.

note.text: Hot rock rises and partly melts, making new ocean crust. Most divergent boundaries are mid-ocean ridges.

steps.title: Ocean plate
steps.instruction: Trace the ocean plate in picture 2, bending down under the land.

note.text: Here plates move together: a convergent boundary. The denser ocean plate sinks under the other. This is subduction.

steps.title: Moving in
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow showing the ocean plate moving.

note.text: A deep ocean trench forms where the plate bends down.

steps.title: Continent
steps.instruction: Trace the continent and its volcano.

note.text: The sinking plate releases water that helps melt rock, building a chain of volcanic mountains like the Andes.

steps.title: Magma
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of magma rising to the volcano.

note.text: Convergent boundaries have many of Earth's big earthquakes and volcanoes.

steps.title: Sliding plates
steps.instruction: Trace picture 3, seen from above, and the boundary line across it.

note.text: Here plates slide past each other: a transform boundary. No crust is made or destroyed.

steps.title: Sliding past
steps.instruction: Draw the two arrows pointing opposite ways.

note.text: The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary. Plates sticking and slipping cause earthquakes.

steps.title: Name the boundaries
steps.instruction: Pick the type of boundary in each picture.

mistakes.Convergent: The arrows point away from each other, so the plates move apart: divergent.

mistakes.Divergent: One plate sinks under the other here, so they're moving together: convergent.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.question: Scientists find a deep trench beside a line of volcanoes. What does this tell them?

options.text: Two plates are coming together, and one is sinking under the other
options.feedback: Yes. A trench and a chain of volcanoes are evidence of a convergent boundary, like the one in picture 2.
Spreading plates make a ridge with new crust, not a trench beside volcanoes.

options.text: The plates are sliding past each other
options.feedback: Transform boundaries don't make trenches or volcanic chains.
Trenches and volcanoes form because plates move: here, one sinks under another.

steps.title: New crust
steps.question: At which boundary is new ocean crust made?

options.feedback: Right. Magma rises between the separating plates and cools into new crust.
At convergent boundaries crust sinks and is destroyed. New crust forms where plates pull apart.
Transform boundaries neither make nor destroy crust.
Only divergent boundaries make new crust.
